subject: PHS
vignette: A 55-year-old woman with newly diagnosed metastatic colon cancer is beginning first-line chemotherapy. She reports significant pain and chemotherapy-associated nausea and asks what help is available for her symptoms. Her oncologist estimates her median survival at 2–3 years, and she strongly wishes to continue cancer-directed treatment.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.text: Enroll the patient in hospice care and discontinue chemotherapy.
Refer the patient for palliative care to be provided concurrently with her ongoing chemotherapy.
Postpone any symptom-focused intervention until chemotherapy is completed.
Reassure the patient that her symptoms are expected and will resolve on their own.
Refer the patient only to a social worker, since symptom management is not a medical service.

explanation_correct: Palliative care aims to provide comfort, relieve suffering, and improve quality of life in patients with complex or life-threatening illness regardless of their diagnosis or prognosis, and it is often delivered concurrently with curative or life-prolonging treatment. This patient has a life-threatening illness, a prognosis measured in years, and an explicit wish to continue chemotherapy — ideal circumstances for concurrent palliative care. It is delivered by an interdisciplinary team (eg, physicians, nurses, social workers) in hospitals, outpatient clinics, or at home.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hospice care is for patients with a prognosis ≤6 months when curative or life-prolonging treatment is no longer wanted or beneficial; this patient has a 2–3 year estimated survival and actively wants continued chemotherapy.
explanation_incorrect.C: Withholding symptom relief until treatment finishes is unnecessary; palliative care is specifically designed to run concurrently with life-prolonging therapy rather than after it.
explanation_incorrect.D: Falsely reassuring the patient dismisses treatable pain and nausea and squanders an opportunity to improve her quality of life during treatment.
explanation_incorrect.E: Palliative care is a medical service delivered by an interdisciplinary team that includes physicians and nurses, not solely a social work referral; reducing it to social work alone undercuts the patient's symptom care.

educationalObjective: Palliative care relieves suffering and improves quality of life regardless of prognosis and is often delivered concurrently with curative or life-prolonging treatment.

subject: PHS
vignette: A 78-year-old man with end-stage heart failure has an estimated prognosis of 2–4 months despite maximal guideline-directed therapy. After a detailed discussion, he decides he no longer wants further hospitalizations or device interventions and wishes to remain at home with his family, focusing on comfort.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.text: Schedule weekly hospital infusions and repeat echocardiography to extend his survival.
Begin palliative care visits while scheduling his defibrillator replacement procedure.
Transfer him to a skilled nursing facility for intensive physical rehabilitation.
Enroll him in hospice (end-of-life) care, since his prognosis is ≤6 months and he no longer wants disease-directed treatment.
Discharge him home without any follow-up plan, since no further interventions are indicated.

explanation_correct: Hospice (end-of-life) care is a form of palliative care for patients with a prognosis ≤6 months when curative or life-prolonging treatment is no longer wanted or beneficial. This patient's estimated survival of 2–4 months and his explicit refusal of further disease-directed interventions satisfy both criteria exactly. Hospice redirects care toward comfort, typically at home, in line with his wishes.

explanation_incorrect.A: Aggressive infusions and serial testing are life-prolonging measures the patient has declined, and his prognosis of months makes them inconsistent with his stated goals of comfort at home.
explanation_incorrect.B: Although palliative care alone would be appropriate at any stage, this patient has declined device interventions and has a prognosis ≤6 months, making hospice the more specific and appropriate next step.
explanation_incorrect.C: Intensive rehabilitation pursues functional recovery and prolongation-oriented goals that contradict the patient's decision to forgo further disease-directed care.
explanation_incorrect.E: Discharging without follow-up abandons the patient; hospice provides structured, interdisciplinary end-of-life support at home rather than no care at all.

educationalObjective: Hospice is appropriate when prognosis is ≤6 months and curative or life-prolonging treatment is no longer wanted or beneficial.

subject: PHS
vignette: A 60-year-old man with severe COPD is recovering from his third exacerbation this year. He expects to live for many years, wants better control of his dyspnea and anxiety, and plans to continue pulmonary rehabilitation and smoking-cessation efforts. His physician plans to involve a team of physicians, nurses, and a social worker to support him.
question: Which of the following features best characterizes the service the physician is arranging for this patient?

options.text: It requires a documented prognosis of ≤6 months.
It is available only to patients hospitalized in inpatient settings.
It must be stopped if the patient begins or continues disease-directed treatment.
It can be delivered only by a single physician acting alone.
It aims to provide comfort, relieve suffering, and improve quality of life regardless of diagnosis or prognosis.

explanation_correct: Palliative care is medical care aiming to provide comfort, relieve suffering, and improve quality of life in patients with complex or life-threatening illness regardless of their diagnosis or prognosis, and it is often concurrent with curative or life-prolonging treatment. This patient's prognosis of years, ongoing disease-directed efforts, and desire for symptom control make palliative care — not hospice — the fitting service. It is delivered by an interdisciplinary team in hospitals, outpatient clinics, or at home.

explanation_incorrect.A: A prognosis ≤6 months is the criterion for hospice care, a distinct subset of palliative care; palliative care itself applies regardless of prognosis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Palliative care is delivered in hospitals, outpatient clinics, or at home, so restricting it to inpatient settings is incorrect.
explanation_incorrect.C: Palliative care is often concurrent with curative or life-prolonging treatment; it does not need to be stopped when such treatment continues, as this patient's continued rehabilitation illustrates.
explanation_incorrect.D: Palliative care is delivered by an interdisciplinary team (eg, physicians, nurses, social workers), not by a single physician working alone.

educationalObjective: Palliative care provides comfort and improves quality of life regardless of diagnosis or prognosis and may run concurrently with disease-directed treatment.
